title: Model families & selection
scopeHtml: Open-weight vs closed APIs, licenses, sizing, price/latency/quality, quantization, routing, deprecation risk, eval-driven choice, compliance. All prices in this chunk are illustrative round numbers unless marked; check current provider pricing pages.

questions.promptHtml: People say "open-source LLM". What do they usually mean, and how is that different from an open-weight model or a closed API model?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you use the terms precisely; the distinction drives legal, deployment and customization decisions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Closed API means I only get an endpoint; weights, training data and code stay with the vendor. Open-weight means the trained weights are downloadable, so I can host, fine-tune and inspect them, but usually not the training data or full recipe, and the license may restrict use. Truly open-source in the OSI sense would also need an OSI-approved license and ideally open data and code. Most 'open-source LLMs' are really open-weight, so I read the license before assuming anything."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three separate axes get blurred:

Axis Closed API Open-weight Fully open (data+code+weights)
Weights downloadable No Yes Yes
Training data/recipe No Usually no Yes
License ToS Varies: Apache/MIT to custom Permissive
Who runs GPUs Vendor You or a host You or a host

Key nuance: "open-weight" says nothing about where it runs. You can call an open-weight model through a hosted API (a third-party inference provider) and never touch a GPU. And a closed model can run inside your cloud account via a cloud marketplace, which changes the data-residency story but not your access to weights.

Why it matters at runtime: with weights you control the version (it never changes under you), can quantize, fine-tune, add custom decoding constraints and read logits. With an API you get what the vendor exposes (maybe logprobs, maybe not) and the vendor can change or retire the model.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable (conceptual).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating "open-weight" with "free to use commercially"; the license decides.
  • Equating "open-weight" with "self-hosted"; hosted open-weight APIs exist.
  • Saying open-weight means reproducible: without data and recipe you cannot retrain it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Llama open source? → By the OSI definition no; it is open-weight under a custom community license with use and scale conditions.
  2. Can I fine-tune an open-weight model? → Usually yes, but the license may impose naming/attribution rules on derivatives.
  3. If weights are open, why might a team still choose a closed API? → Frontier capability, no ops burden, faster iteration; self-hosting has a fixed GPU and on-call cost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "open models are free, closed are paid." Senior: separates weights access, license, and runtime location, and treats each as an independent decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team told compliance "we use open source" and later found the license barred a use case; the audit cost weeks.

questions.promptHtml: What are the main factors you weigh when choosing between a closed API model and a self-hosted open-weight model?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests structured trade-off thinking instead of ideology.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I weigh six things: capability on my task, cost at my volume, data privacy and residency, control and customization, latency and reliability, and lock-in or deprecation risk. Closed APIs usually win on peak capability and zero ops. Open-weight wins on data control, version stability, deep customization and cost at sustained high volume. I decide on an eval of my own task, and often end up hybrid."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Capability: frontier closed models often lead on hard reasoning; open-weight models are often good enough for classification, extraction, summarization. Measure, do not assume.
  • Cost: API cost is variable (per token); self-hosting is mostly fixed (GPU hours) plus engineering. Break-even depends on utilization (see Q150).
  • Privacy/residency: self-hosting keeps data in your VPC; many closed vendors offer zero-retention, regional endpoints or cloud-hosted variants that may be enough (see Q158).
  • Control: open weights allow LoRA/full fine-tuning, custom quantization, constrained decoding, pinning an exact checkpoint forever.
  • Reliability/latency: APIs have rate limits and shared-capacity variance; self-hosting gives predictable latency if you size correctly but you own the pager.
  • Lock-in: closed means prompts tuned to one model's quirks and a retirement clock; open means you own the checkpoint but not the serving stack skills.
Need frontier reasoning, low volume, small team  -> closed API
Strict data boundary / air-gap                   -> self-host open-weight
High steady volume, narrow task                  -> small tuned open model
Unknown                                          -> prototype closed, measure, then decide

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Comparing list price per token without counting engineering, idle GPU time, and eval cost.
  • Deciding on a public leaderboard rather than your task.
  • Ignoring that hosted open-weight APIs give a middle path.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does hybrid make sense? → Route easy/high-volume traffic to a small open model, hard cases to a frontier API.
  2. What would make you switch later? → Volume growth, a compliance requirement, or a deprecation notice.
  3. How do you keep switching cheap? → Provider-agnostic interface, prompts under version control, and a regression eval suite (Q156).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists pros/cons. Senior ties each axis to a measurable number (eval score, $/1k requests, p95, compliance requirement) and names the trigger that flips the decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Startups often start on a closed API for speed, then move one high-volume workload to open weights once its quality floor is known.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the main license families you see on LLM weights: Apache 2.0/MIT, Llama-style community licenses, and OpenRAIL. What do they allow and restrict?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Licensing mistakes are a real blocker at product companies; seniors are expected to check it before building.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Apache 2.0 and MIT are permissive: commercial use, modification and redistribution allowed with notice/attribution, and Apache adds an explicit patent grant. Llama-style community licenses are custom: broadly commercial but with conditions like attribution, naming rules, an acceptable-use policy, and a large-scale user threshold. OpenRAIL licenses add behavioral-use restrictions, such as banned harmful uses, that must flow down to derivatives. I always read the specific model's license file, since families mix licenses by size and version."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Family Commercial use Redistribute derivatives Use restrictions Typical obligations
MIT Yes Yes None Keep copyright notice
Apache 2.0 Yes Yes None Notice, state changes, patent grant
Llama community (custom) Yes, with conditions Yes, with conditions Acceptable-use policy; scale threshold Attribution, naming, license copy
OpenRAIL-style Generally yes Yes, restrictions flow down Behavioral-use clauses Pass restrictions to downstream users
Research/non-commercial No Limited Research only Need separate commercial license

Per the research I did: some vendors ship the same family under different licenses (e.g. one comparison reports Mistral models mostly Apache 2.0 with some older large models under a research license, and Qwen variants differing by version). I did not verify the primary texts, so the rule is: check the license file on the exact checkpoint.

Runtime relevance: a license is a deployment constraint like a dependency's license. It must be tracked in your model registry the same way you track code dependencies.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Not applicable (a registry entry is conceptual):

MODEL_REGISTRY = {
    "org/model-7b": {"license": "apache-2.0", "commercial": True, "checked": "2026-10-01"},
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trusting the family name; license can differ per checkpoint.
  • Forgetting that fine-tuned derivatives inherit obligations.
  • Assuming a gated download on Hugging Face means non-commercial.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Apache 2.0 cover training data? → No; it licenses the weights/code as published, not the data copyright questions.
  2. What does a behavioral-use clause mean for a SaaS? → You must flow the restrictions to your users via ToS.
  3. Who decides if my use is allowed? → Legal; engineering supplies the facts (model, use, scale, distribution).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Apache is free, Llama is mostly free." Senior: maintains a license registry, knows obligations differ for hosting vs distributing, and escalates edge cases to legal early.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped a fine-tuned model to customers on-prem and only then discovered redistribution triggered attribution and naming obligations.

questions.promptHtml: If you build a commercial product on a Llama 3.x model, what obligations does the community license put on you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Concrete test of whether you have actually read a license rather than waving at "open source".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "From the Llama 3.1 community license text I looked at: you must include a copy of the agreement when distributing, show 'Built with Llama' on related product surfaces, start derivative model names with 'Llama', keep the notice file, and if your products exceed 700 million monthly active users you must request a license from Meta. There's also an acceptable-use policy. Versions differ, so I'd verify the version I'm actually deploying and have legal sign off."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The points above come from copies of the Llama 3.1 license (released 2024-07-23) mirrored on Hugging Face, not Meta's own site, so treat as "verify against Meta's current text". Later Llama versions have their own licenses, and terms (including any regional restrictions for multimodal models) change by version.

Practical mapping:

  • Hosting for your own users (SaaS): mostly attribution and AUP compliance; you are not redistributing weights.
  • Shipping weights to customers (on-prem, edge): you are distributing; include the license copy and notice.
  • Releasing a fine-tune publicly: naming rule plus license inheritance.
  • Using Llama outputs to train another model: check the specific version's clause; earlier versions restricted this, later ones relaxed it. Verify.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating the 700M MAU clause as irrelevant and so skipping the rest.
  • Remembering Llama 2's terms for Llama 3.x.
  • Not recording which license version each deployed checkpoint came under.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the MAU threshold include affiliates? → The text refers to the licensee and its affiliates; legal confirms.
  2. Is a distilled student model a derivative? → Treat it as one and check the clause on using outputs/weights; verify per version.
  3. How would you operationalize compliance? → Registry entry per checkpoint, CI check that required attribution strings exist in docs/UI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "It's free unless you're huge." Senior: lists attribution, naming, AUP and version dependence, and distinguishes hosting from distributing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Missing attribution in on-prem customer docs surfaced in a vendor security questionnaire and had to be patched into release notes.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide how big a model a task needs? Walk through how you would match model size to task.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Over-buying the biggest model is the most common cost mistake; seniors size by evidence.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I classify the task by how much reasoning, world knowledge and instruction nuance it needs. Classification, extraction, routing, and short summarization often work on small models, especially with few-shot or light fine-tuning. Multi-step reasoning, ambiguous instructions, long-horizon agents and open-ended writing need larger or reasoning models. I start with the cheapest model that might work, build a labeled eval set, and move up only until quality meets the bar."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Capability scales with parameters and training data, but task-specific needs differ:

Task Typical starting size Why
Intent classification, PII tagging Small (1-8B) or tuned encoder Narrow label space
Structured extraction from clean text Small-mid Pattern following
Summarization Small-mid Faithfulness mostly needs context handling
RAG answer synthesis Mid Needs grounding discipline
Multi-step reasoning, code, planning Large / reasoning Needs depth
Agentic tool use Large Error compounding across steps

Memory sizing helper: weights bytes ~ params x bytes per param. A 70B model at FP16 = 70e9 x 2 = 140 GB (needs multiple GPUs), at 4-bit about 70e9 x 0.5 = 35 GB plus KV cache. An 8B model at FP16 = 16 GB fits one 24 GB GPU. So size also decides your hardware class.

Method: write 100-300 labeled examples from real traffic, run the ladder small -> mid -> large, plot score vs $ per 1k requests, pick the knee.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def pick_model(candidates, eval_set, bar, run):
    # candidates sorted cheapest -> most expensive
    for m in candidates:
        score = sum(run(m, x) == x["label"] for x in eval_set) / len(eval_set)
        if score >= bar:
            return m, score
    return None, 0.0

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Picking by parameter count across different families and generations; a newer 8B can beat an older 70B on some tasks.
  • Ignoring the KV cache and context length when estimating memory.
  • Testing on easy hand-picked prompts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does fine-tuning a small model beat a large prompt? → Narrow, stable task with enough labels and high volume (details in C6).
  2. Why can a smaller model be better for you? → Latency, cost, on-device or data-boundary constraints.
  3. What if quality needs differ by request difficulty? → Route (Q154).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "bigger is better, use GPT-class for all." Senior: ladder eval, cost-quality knee, memory math, and hardware class implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support-tagging service ran a frontier model for a 12-label classification; a small tuned model matched accuracy within noise at a fraction of the cost.

questions.promptHtml: How do latency, price and quality trade off when picking an LLM, and how do you reason about each quantitatively?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors must convert vague "fast and cheap and good" into numbers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Price is input tokens times input rate plus output tokens times output rate, and output is usually several times pricier per token. Latency is time to first token, driven by prompt size and queueing, plus output tokens times per-token decode time, so long outputs dominate. Quality is task eval score. Bigger models cost more and decode slower; reasoning models spend hidden thinking tokens, raising both cost and latency. I plot candidates on a cost-latency-quality chart and pick from the Pareto frontier for the product's SLA."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cost per request = (in_tokens x in_price + out_tokens x out_price) / 1e6. Illustrative prices (not real): Model A $0.15 in / $0.60 out per 1M; Model B $3 in / $15 out per 1M. For 2,000 in / 300 out:

  • A: (2000x0.15 + 300x0.60)/1e6 = (300+180)/1e6 = $0.00048
  • B: (2000x3 + 300x15)/1e6 = (6000+4500)/1e6 = $0.0105 (about 22x)

Latency model: total = queue + TTFT + out_tokens x TPOT. If TPOT is 25 ms, 300 output tokens add 7.5 s; trimming output to 100 tokens saves 5 s, often more than switching models. Prompt caching lowers input cost and TTFT for shared prefixes where the provider supports it (details C2).

Quality has a threshold nature: below the bar the output is worthless, above it extra quality has diminishing product value. So choose the cheapest/fastest model clearing the bar.

quality ^        B  *
        |   A  *
        |  *
        +---------------> cost/latency
Pareto: keep only points not dominated on all three

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def cost(in_tok, out_tok, p_in, p_out):  # prices per 1M tokens
    return (in_tok * p_in + out_tok * p_out) / 1e6

print(cost(2000, 300, 0.15, 0.60))  # 0.00048
print(cost(2000, 300, 3.0, 15.0))   # 0.0105

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using only input price; output tokens often dominate cost.
  • Ignoring reasoning/hidden tokens billed as output.
  • Comparing average latency instead of p95/p99.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reduce latency without changing model? → Shorter outputs, streaming, caching, smaller prompts, parallel calls.
  2. When is more expensive actually cheaper? → If the cheaper model needs retries or human review.
  3. How do you set the bar? → Tie to product metric (accept rate, escalation rate), not abstract score.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE quotes per-token price. Senior computes cost per successful task including retries and review, and models p95 latency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team cut p95 from 9 s to 4 s by capping output length, with no model change.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B support platform wants to auto-triage 2.4M tickets/month into 14 categories and a priority level. Average ticket is 600 input tokens; output is a short JSON of about 40 tokens. The prototype uses a frontier closed model at (illustrative) $3 in / $15 out per 1M tokens and scores 94% accuracy on 500 hand-labeled tickets. Finance flags the projected bill. Target p95 under 2 s. Legal says tickets may contain customer PII but a zero-retention API is acceptable. A teammate proposes "just use the cheapest open model".
questions.promptHtml: How do you choose the model for production?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks the cheapest model by price list or sticks with the frontier model "because it scores best", without an eval ladder, cost math, or latency check.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What accuracy is the bar and what does an error cost (misroute vs wrong priority)? Is the 500-ticket sample representative (languages, channels)? Is there label history for tuning? What is peak QPS vs average? Can low-confidence tickets go to a human?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Not an incident.) Baseline cost: per ticket (600x3 + 40x15)/1e6 = $0.0024; x 2.4M = about $5,760/month.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A small model with few-shot hits 92-94%; (b) a small model fine-tuned on historical labels hits parity; (c) a cascade: small first, frontier on low confidence.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run 3-4 candidates (small open, mid closed, frontier) on a bigger stratified set (2,000 tickets, oversampling rare categories); report per-class F1, not just accuracy; measure p95 under load; get logprobs or a self-reported confidence for the cascade.
  5. Root cause: The cost is from using a frontier model on a task with a narrow label space.
  6. Fix: Suppose a small model at $0.15 in / $0.60 out: (600x0.15 + 40x0.6)/1e6 = $0.000114 per ticket -> about $274/month, if it clears the bar. If it reaches 91% and the bar is 93%, route the lowest-confidence ~15% to the frontier model: 0.85x$0.000114 + 0.15x$0.0024 = about $0.00046 -> roughly $1,100/month.
  7. Prevention: Keep the eval set as a regression gate; alert on category-distribution drift and escalation rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not self-host for a sub-$6k/month bill: a GPU node plus on-call costs more. I would not pick on price list alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Volume grows 20x to 48M/month? -> Frontier cost goes to about $115k/month; self-hosting a tuned small model becomes worth a break-even analysis (Q150).
  • Accuracy is fine but one rare high-priority class has low recall? -> Class-specific threshold or rule-based escalation for that class.
  • Tickets are 40% non-English? -> Stratify eval by language; small models often degrade more there.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A triage system moved to a small model after a ladder eval; the first week looked great until a rare "outage" class had 60% recall. A one-line routing rule for outage keywords closed the gap.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses by price or brand; no eval; no math.
  • Hire: ladder eval, cost math, and a cascade or small-model proposal.
  • Strong hire: per-class metrics, stratified eval, break-even awareness, and risk-aware escalation design.

questions.contextHtml: A document-tagging service calls a mid-tier closed API (illustrative $0.50 in / $1.50 out per 1M tokens). It processes 2.0B input and 0.4B output tokens a month. The CTO asks whether to self-host an open-weight 8B model instead. Quoted GPU cost: $2.00/hour per GPU on-demand (illustrative). Load testing shows one GPU sustains about 1,500 output tokens/s aggregate with batching at the latency target (assumption, measure yourself). Traffic is business-hours heavy: peak is 4x the overnight average. One platform engineer is available at about 30% time.
questions.promptHtml: Does self-hosting pay off? Show the math and what else you need to know.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "GPUs are cheaper than API tokens" with no utilization, peak-to-average, or ops cost. Or compares the API bill to one GPU's monthly cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is quality of the 8B equal to the API model on our eval? Is traffic latency-sensitive or batchable overnight? What are the availability needs (so I need N+1 replicas)? Is data residency a driver? Who is on call?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Not an incident.) First cheap wins on the API: prompt caching for the shared instruction prefix, shorter outputs, batch API for non-urgent jobs where the vendor offers it (verify discounts).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) API stays cheaper at this volume; (b) self-host wins only above some volume or with batch-friendly traffic; (c) quality gap kills it regardless.
  4. How I'd verify each: API cost: 2000 x $0.50 + 400 x $1.50 = $1,000 + $600 = $1,600/month. Self-host capacity: 0.4B output tokens/month / (30x86,400 s) = about 154 tok/s average; at 4x peak = about 617 tok/s, so one GPU covers peak in raw throughput. But I need at least 2 for redundancy: 2 x $2 x 730 h = $2,920/month. Prefill for 2.0B input tokens also takes GPU time; I would load-test with real prompts, not assume.
  5. Root cause: The question is utilization: two GPUs run mostly idle at this scale, so fixed cost exceeds the variable API cost.
  6. Fix: Stay on the API now. Compute break-even: at a 10x volume ($16,000/month API), a fleet of about 6 GPUs ($8,760/month) plus engineer time could win, if the 8B matches quality. Revisit at that point or when compliance forces it.
  7. Prevention: Track cost per 1k tasks and tokens/month; set a re-evaluation trigger at an agreed spend level.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not self-host for a $1.6k bill. Hidden costs: engineer time, model upgrades, security patching, autoscaling lag, and eval re-runs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Traffic can be batched overnight? -> Spot or scheduled GPUs and queued processing sharply improve utilization; break-even moves lower.
  • The 8B scores 4 points lower? -> Fine-tune or cascade; otherwise the savings are fictional.
  • Vendor cuts prices 50%? -> Break-even volume doubles; another reason to avoid premature infra.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team bought reserved GPUs for a launch forecast of 5x the real traffic. Utilization hovered at 12% for months, so effective cost per token was several times the API price.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: compares token price to GPU price; no utilization.
  • Hire: monthly math for both, peak vs average, redundancy.
  • Strong hire: includes ops cost, quality parity gate, batching, and an explicit re-evaluation trigger.

questions.promptHtml: When choosing a deployment model, how does quantization level (FP16, FP8, INT8, 4-bit) affect quality and cost, and how would you decide?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quantization is how teams fit bigger models on fewer GPUs; seniors know it is not free and must be validated per task. (Deep treatment is in C2.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Quantization stores weights, and sometimes activations, in fewer bits to cut memory and often speed up serving. From the studies I read, 8-bit and FP8 are close to lossless, while 4-bit weight-only methods show small average drops that grow on long context and non-English tasks. So I treat FP8/INT8 as the safe default, and 4-bit as a decision I validate on my own eval set, especially for long inputs, multilingual, and reasoning-heavy tasks."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Memory for weights = params x bits / 8. A 70B model: FP16 140 GB, 8-bit 70 GB, 4-bit about 35 GB (plus quantization metadata and KV cache). So 4-bit may turn a 4-GPU deployment into 1-2 GPUs.

Evidence I read: a large study of quantized Llama 3.1 models ("Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death?") reports FP8 essentially lossless and W8A8-INT within roughly 1-3% per-task on average; a long-context study reports average drops of 0.2% (FP8), 0.8% (GPTQ-int8), 1.8% (AWQ), 2.7% (GPTQ-int4), 6.9% (BNB-nf4), with much larger drops on some long-context tasks and bigger damage for non-English. Treat these as indicative, not guarantees; results vary by model, method and hyperparameters.

Key distinction: weight-only quantization saves memory (helps memory-bound decode); weight+activation (W8A8) also speeds compute-bound prefill on hardware that supports it. Also: KV-cache quantization is a separate knob with its own quality impact.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Compare a quantized and reference model on YOUR eval before shipping
def regression(ref_scores, q_scores, tol=0.02):
    drop = sum(ref_scores)/len(ref_scores) - sum(q_scores)/len(q_scores)
    return drop <= tol  # also report per-slice: language, length bucket

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trusting a public perplexity or MMLU number; task-specific degradation can be larger.
  • Not slicing by context length or language.
  • Forgetting KV cache memory is independent of weight bit-width.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a quantized bigger model better than an unquantized smaller one? → Often at 8-bit, sometimes at 4-bit, but test; it is task dependent.
  2. Why might 4-bit hurt long context? → Errors accumulate over long dependencies; the studies show larger drops there.
  3. Does quantization change safety behavior? → It can; re-run safety evals on the quantized artifact.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "4-bit loses a little accuracy." Senior: gives bit-width memory math, distinguishes weight-only from W8A8, and demands slice-level eval.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 4-bit deployment passed the overall eval but regressed on a non-English slice that was 15% of traffic.

questions.promptHtml: Why shouldn't you pick a model based on public leaderboards, and what do you do instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Eval discipline is the biggest differentiator between senior and junior GenAI engineers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Public benchmarks measure someone else's tasks, can be contaminated by training data, are gamed or overfit, and ignore my latency, cost, format and language needs. I use leaderboards only to shortlist, then build a task-specific eval from real production-like inputs with a rubric or labels, run 3-5 candidates under the same prompt budget, and choose on quality, cost and p95 together with confidence intervals."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problems with leaderboards: (1) contamination: test questions leak into pretraining; (2) Goodhart: models are tuned to the benchmark; (3) aggregate scores hide per-task variance; (4) preference arenas reward style and length; (5) saturation: top models are within noise; (6) prompt sensitivity: scores depend on the harness.

Process:

  1. Collect 200-500 real inputs, stratified by difficulty and slice.
  2. Define the pass criteria (exact match, schema validity, rubric graded by calibrated LLM judge plus human spot checks).
  3. Run candidates with prompts tuned fairly for each (not one model's prompt).
  4. Report mean with bootstrap CI, per-slice results, cost per success, p95 latency.
  5. Re-run on every model change.

Statistical note: with n=200 and p=0.9, standard error is sqrt(0.9x0.1/200) = 0.021, so a 2-point gap is noise.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import random
def bootstrap_ci(scores, n=2000):
    means = sorted(sum(random.choices(scores, k=len(scores)))/len(scores) for _ in range(n))
    return means[int(0.025*n)], means[int(0.975*n)]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using one prompt tuned for the incumbent model.
  • Eval set built from the same examples used in the prompt.
  • Using an LLM judge from the same family as a candidate without checking bias.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How big should the eval set be? → Large enough that your decision gap exceeds the CI; start with 200-500, grow on disagreements.
  2. How do you handle subjective tasks? → Pairwise comparison with a rubric and human calibration (details in C7).
  3. How do you detect contamination? → Perturb benchmark items or use fresh private tasks; compare public vs private score gap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "I check MMLU and LMArena." Senior: builds a private stratified eval with CIs and cost/latency, and treats it as a CI gate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A top-ranked model lost to a mid-ranked one on a team's invoice-extraction eval because of stricter JSON adherence.

questions.contextHtml:
A gateway wraps two models to improve availability: a primary with a 128k context window and a cheaper fallback with an 8k window. After launch, support reports empty answers on long documents, and the bill is 1.4x expected. Logs show repeated primary: 400 context_length_exceeded then fallback: 400 context_length_exceeded for 3% of requests, plus primary: timeout bursts followed by fallback success with noticeably worse answers. Code (pseudo-SDK, client.chat stands for any provider SDK):

MODELS = ["big-128k", "small-8k"]

def complete(messages):
    for model in MODELS:
        try:
            r = client.chat(model=model, messages=messages, timeout=5)
            return r.text
        except Exception:
            continue
    return ""
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add logging." Misses that catching everything retries non-retryable errors and the silent empty-string return.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are quality and context equivalent across the models? Is the 5 s timeout appropriate for long outputs? Are failures primarily rate limits, timeouts or 5xx? Are retries billed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return an explicit error for non-retryable cases instead of "", and disable fallback for requests exceeding the fallback window.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) bare except Exception swallows 400/401 errors; (b) fallback context is smaller than the request; (c) 5 s timeout too short for long generations and kills requests the primary would finish, which are still billed partially; (d) silent "" hides failures from monitoring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count error classes in logs; compare token counts of failed requests to 8k; check provider billing for aborted requests; compare eval scores for fallback-served traffic.
  5. Root cause: The code treats all failures as transient, ignores capability differences, and hides terminal failure.
  6. Fix:
RETRYABLE = (TimeoutError, ConnectionError)  # plus provider's 429/5xx classes

def complete(messages, est_tokens):
    errs = []
    for m in MODELS:
        if est_tokens > m.context - m.max_out:
            continue  # model can't serve this request
        try:
            return client.chat(model=m.name, messages=messages, timeout=m.timeout)
        except RETRYABLE as e:
            errs.append((m.name, e)); metrics.incr("fallback", model=m.name)
    raise LLMUnavailable(errs)  # never return ""

Plus jittered retry on the same model for 429, and a different strategy (truncate/summarize/reject) for long inputs. 7. Prevention: Tests with oversize inputs, a chaos test that kills the primary, an alert on fallback rate, and per-model eval for fallback quality. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not silently fall back to a model that cannot meet the quality bar; for some products an honest error beats a degraded answer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fallback is a different vendor? -> Prompt and tool-schema differences; keep an adapter and test the fallback prompt separately.
  • Provider-wide outage? -> Circuit breaker so you stop paying timeouts on a dead primary.
  • Cost doubling from retries? -> Cap attempts and use hedged requests only for latency-critical paths.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An outage drill revealed the fallback model had a different JSON tool-call format; every fallback response failed parsing, so "availability" was effectively zero during the incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds logging.
  • Hire: spots bare except, empty return, and context mismatch.
  • Strong hire: adds capability-aware routing, circuit breakers, fallback eval, and discusses degraded-answer policy.

questions.promptHtml: Explain multi-model routing. How do routers, cascades and static rules differ, and what can go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Routing is the main cost-lever at scale; seniors must know the failure modes, not just the idea.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. A static rule routes by task type. A learned router predicts, before generating, whether a strong or weak model is needed. A cascade tries the cheap model first and escalates if a confidence check fails, costing extra for escalated requests. Wins are real but depend on the router's accuracy and the confidence signal, so I measure routing quality against an eval and monitor drift."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Static rules: by endpoint, user tier, input length, detected language. Predictable, cheap, debuggable.
  • Learned router (RouteLLM-style): per the paper (Ong et al., 2024), routers trained on human preference data decide between a strong and weak model per query; the project reports large savings on some benchmarks (e.g. over 85% on MT Bench, 45% MMLU, 35% GSM8K at a quality target), which are benchmark-specific, so verify on your own traffic.
  • Cascade (FrugalGPT-style): query models in order until an answer passes a reliability check; cost grows for hard queries because you pay for each tried model. I did not read the paper's headline savings figure in primary form; verify before quoting.

Cost model for a cascade: E[cost] = c_small + p_escalate x c_big. If c_small = 0.1, c_big = 1.0 (relative), p = 0.2: 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3, a 70% saving, if quality holds. If p = 0.9 the cascade costs 1.0 and is slower than always using the big model.

Failure modes: confidence from LLM self-reports is poorly calibrated; router trained on a different traffic distribution; latency added by the extra hop; inconsistent style between models confuses users; hard to debug "why did this get the small model"; routers can fail on rare high-stakes inputs.

request -> [router/classifier] -> small model -> [verifier] -pass-> answer
                    \                               \-fail-> big model -> answer

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def cascade(q, small, big, verify, threshold=0.8):
    a, conf = small(q)
    if conf >= threshold and verify(q, a):
        return a, "small"
    return big(q)[0], "big"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Routing on prompt length only and calling it "intelligent".
  • Not logging which model served each request, so quality regressions are untraceable.
  • Never re-evaluating the router when traffic shifts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Router vs cascade latency? → Router adds one cheap hop but one generation; a cascade adds a full generation for escalated requests.
  2. How do you get a reliable confidence? → Verifiers (schema/tests/retrieval check), logprobs where available, calibration on labeled data.
  3. How do you evaluate a router? → Quality vs cost curve on held-out traffic, plus per-slice and high-stakes recall.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "send easy stuff to cheap model." Senior: models expected cost with escalation rate, handles calibration, monitors drift, and keeps an audit trail.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A routing layer saved cost until a new product feature shifted traffic toward hard prompts, the escalation rate hit 70%, and latency doubled.

questions.contextHtml: A contract-analysis product calls model="provider-large-latest". Monday 09:10 the extraction accuracy dashboard (daily eval on 300 canned contracts) drops from 93% to 81%. Customer tickets mention "missing clauses" and malformed JSON. No deploy happened in 5 days. API error rate is normal; p95 latency is up from 3.1 s to 4.4 s; mean output tokens rose from 410 to 640. A teammate suspects the vector DB (red herring: the product does not use RAG for this feature); another suspects a prompt injection in a customer file.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you respond?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts debugging the vector DB or code, never checks for model/version change, and has no rollback because everything is on a floating alias.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the response metadata include the resolved model version? Did the provider announce an alias update? Is degradation uniform across customers or concentrated in certain formats? Is the canned eval run with temperature 0 and a fixed seed where supported?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin to the last known-good dated snapshot if still available; otherwise switch to the prior vendor model or a prompt hotfix. Announce degraded status to support.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) the -latest alias now points to a new snapshot with different behavior (verbosity, format following); (2) provider-side infra/quantization or sampling-default change (cannot see, but check status page); (3) our input distribution shifted (a new customer's scanned docs); (4) prompt injection in a file (affects one customer, not the canned eval); (5) tokenizer or SDK change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check the resolved model id in responses/logs for the date of the change; rerun the canned eval on pinned old snapshot vs alias side by side; diff outputs on the same 20 failures; compare output token distributions (410 -> 640 suggests chattier style, possibly breaking JSON); look at the provider changelog.
  5. Root cause: The alias moved to a new snapshot; the new model over-explains and breaks the strict JSON/clauses format our prompt relied on. The canned eval caught it only after-the-fact since it runs daily, not at change time.
  6. Fix: Short term: pin the snapshot id; add explicit format constraints (structured outputs / schema mode if supported) and re-tune the prompt on the new model. Long term: deliberate upgrade procedure: shadow traffic, eval gate, canary 5%, then promote.
  7. Prevention: Never use floating aliases in production; log resolved model version per request; run the eval hourly or on version-string change; alert on output-length and JSON-validity drift; subscribe to deprecation/changelog feeds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pinning means you eventually face a retirement date, so keep an upgrade runway. I would not rewrite the pipeline or blame the DB before checking the model id.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The old snapshot is retired? -> Fall back to the nearest alternative with eval-gated prompt changes; ask the vendor about extended access.
  • It only happens for 5% of customers? -> Slice by doc type/length; the new model may regress on scanned or long documents.
  • Could the vendor change behavior without changing the model id? -> Possibly (serving or safety layers); only black-box monitoring catches it, which is why you run continuous evals.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team learned about a snapshot change from a customer. After that, they stored the resolved model id with every response and a nightly job diffed output-length distributions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: debugs unrelated components.
  • Hire: identifies alias drift, pins, compares old vs new.
  • Strong hire: adds canary/shadow upgrades, version logging, drift alerts, and a retirement runway.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design for vendor model deprecation and lock-in? What does a good abstraction layer look like and what are its limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Models are retired on a schedule; seniors build for migration from day one without over-engineering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Assume every model will be retired. I pin dated snapshots, track vendor deprecation notices, and keep a thin provider-agnostic interface for the request/response plus an adapter per provider. The real portability work is not the API call; it is prompts, tool schemas, structured-output behavior and evals. So I keep prompts versioned per model and a regression eval suite that lets me swap a model in days with evidence."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Facts from my research: OpenAI's deprecations page says it emails customers actively using a model and documents the retirement; secondary reporting says generally available models get at least about 6 months notice, preview models can get as little as about 2 weeks, and safety-driven retirements can be faster. I could not confirm exact figures from the official page text, so verify with the vendor's current policy. One outlet reported a case with 20 days' notice, which illustrates that policies have exceptions.

What a good layer contains:

  • Normalized request: messages, tools, response schema, max tokens, temperature.
  • Normalized response: text, tool calls, usage, finish reason, resolved model id.
  • Adapters translating roles, system prompt placement, tool-call formats, streaming events, errors.
  • Capability table per model: context window, tool support, JSON mode, vision, max output.

Limits: lowest-common-denominator interfaces hide useful vendor features (caching controls, reasoning settings); prompts that are tuned for one model degrade on another; evals, not interfaces, tell you whether a swap works.

app -> LLMClient(interface) -> Adapter[A|B|C] -> provider
                |-> model registry (id, snapshot, limits, retire date)
                |-> eval gate (golden set) on every model change

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ModelSpec:
    name: str; snapshot: str; context: int; retire_on: str  # ISO date

def check_runway(spec, today, min_days=90):
    from datetime import date
    return (date.fromisoformat(spec.retire_on) - today).days >= min_days

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a gateway library and assuming prompts are now portable.
  • Not tracking retirement dates, learning from a failing prod call.
  • Building a heavy abstraction before a second provider is needed.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Build vs use a gateway (LiteLLM-style, cloud gateways)? → Gateways speed up adapters; you still own prompts, evals, and fallbacks. Evaluate maintenance and security of the gateway.
  2. What do you do 60 days before retirement? → Run the eval on candidates, tune prompts, shadow traffic, canary, promote, and keep rollback until cutover is safe.
  3. How do you handle dedicated fine-tunes on a retiring base? → Fine-tuned models are tied to base-model lifecycle; plan re-training on the new base with stored datasets.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "wrap the SDK in an interface." Senior: knows portability lives in prompts and evals, maintains a model registry with retirement dates, and automates the swap runbook.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A retirement email went to a departed engineer's address; the model died in prod. Now the registry owns a team alias and a 90-day alert.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech chat assistant serves 1,800 req/min peak on a closed API model, average 1,500 input and 250 output tokens. A new compliance rule requires customer text to stay inside the company's cloud account within 6 months. The plan: move to a self-hosted open-weight 70B model. Offline eval: 91% task pass vs 94% for the incumbent. The new stack's p95 is 5.2 s vs 3.0 s. Prompts use the incumbent's tool-call format; 22% of traffic uses tools. No downtime allowed.
questions.promptHtml: How do you run the migration?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Swap the model name and deploy" or a big-bang cutover after a single offline eval.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a compliant managed option (closed model in our cloud region/VPC) that avoids self-hosting? Which behaviors are regulated (all prompts or only PII fields)? Is 3 points of quality acceptable on all slices? What is the capacity budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; the deadline is 6 months. Do a feasibility check on the managed in-VPC option first; it may meet the rule with far less risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The quality gap is mostly prompt/tool-format mismatch and can be closed; (b) the gap is real on hard slices; (c) latency needs more GPUs or a smaller/faster serving config; (d) capacity during peaks is the real risk.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-tune prompts and tool schemas for the new model, re-run eval per slice; load-test at 1.5x peak with realistic length distribution; compute capacity.
  5. Root cause: Not a bug; a platform constraint changing the model class.
  6. Fix (plan): Build an adapter layer; shadow-mirror 100% of traffic to the new stack (responses discarded) and compare automatically; canary 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% by customer cohort with automatic rollback on pass-rate, latency and JSON-validity guardrails; keep the incumbent warm until two stable weeks. Escalate hard slices (tool-heavy, long) to the in-VPC closed option if allowed.
  7. Prevention: Regression suite built from shadow logs; per-slice dashboards; capacity runbook; dual-run for future migrations.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big-bang cutover; not claiming equal quality from averages; not forgetting that PII logs from shadow traffic must remain inside the compliant boundary.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The canary shows p95 6 s at peak? -> Add replicas, tune batching, shorten prompts, or quantize (with a quality re-check).
  • Legal says shadow logs count as processing? -> Mirror to the compliant environment only, mask PII.
  • Rollback needed at 25%? -> Weighted routing flag flips traffic in seconds; incumbent kept warm for this reason.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration looked equal offline but shadow traffic showed the new model refusing 4% of requests the old one answered, due to a different safety tuning. The refusal rate was not in the offline eval.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swap and hope.
  • Hire: shadow plus canary plus rollback.
  • Strong hire: considers managed in-VPC alternative, per-slice guardrails, compliance of shadow data, capacity math.

questions.promptHtml: A customer demands that their data never leave the EU and not be used for training. How do model-selection and deployment choices respond to data residency and compliance requirements?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Enterprise deals hinge on this; seniors map the requirement to concrete architecture options.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I separate four things: where data is processed, where it is stored or logged, whether the vendor may train on it, and who can access it. Options range from a vendor's regional endpoint with zero data retention, to a closed model served inside my cloud account, to self-hosted open weights in my VPC or on-prem. I pick the least costly option that satisfies the legal text, get contractual terms (DPA, subprocessors), and verify with legal; I do not decide compliance alone."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers of control, increasing in strictness and cost:

Option Residency Training use Ops burden
Public API, default terms Vendor-defined Check ToS (API data often not used for training by default at major vendors; verify) None
Regional endpoint + zero retention Regional Contractual Low
Closed model via your cloud tenant (managed) Your region Contractual Low-medium
Self-hosted open weights in VPC Full None High
On-prem/air-gapped Full None Highest

Details seniors cover: logs, traces, eval datasets and vector stores also hold data and must follow the same boundary; third-party tools (observability SaaS, LLM judges) are subprocessors; abuse-monitoring retention windows at vendors (often 30 days unless zero-retention is approved; verify); encryption and access auditing; right-to-delete handling for fine-tuning data; sector rules (HIPAA, GDPR, PCI) that map to attestations (BAA, SOC 2). Model choice also matters: some open-weight licenses restrict regions or uses.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Not applicable; config sketch:

POLICY = {"tenant_eu": {"endpoint": "https://eu.example-provider", "retention": "zero",
                        "log_store": "eu-west-1", "judge_model": "self-hosted"}}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Securing the model call but sending prompts to a US-hosted tracing SaaS.
  • Assuming "no training" equals "no retention".
  • Treating compliance as a one-time checkbox instead of verifiable controls.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does self-hosting automatically make you compliant? → No: you still need access control, logging policy, patching and audits.
  2. How do you prove residency to a customer? → Architecture docs, region-pinned infra-as-code, audit logs, vendor attestations.
  3. How does multi-tenant routing work? → Per-tenant policy decides endpoint, log store and models; enforced at the gateway.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use a self-hosted model." Senior: enumerates the data flows beyond the model call and picks the cheapest compliant tier with legal sign off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deal stalled because eval traces were shipped to an out-of-region observability vendor; the model call itself was compliant.

questions.contextHtml: A legal-tech VP says: "We need the best model for reviewing contracts. Budget is flexible." Facts you can get: 40k contracts/year, average 18k tokens (some 150k), reviewers currently spend 25 minutes per contract, a wrong "no risk" call is costly, and two customers ban sending data to third parties. There is no labeled data yet. Three vendors have pitched benchmark slides. Your team has two engineers and a six-week target.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this into a model-selection decision?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks the model with the highest benchmark number, or says "need more info" and stops.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the output (clause extraction, risk flags, redlines)? What recall is required on high-risk clauses? Is a human always in the loop? Which customers have the no-third-party ban (what exactly is allowed)? What does a missed clause cost vs a false flag?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; define "best" as a measurable target: recall >= X on a defined clause set, precision high enough to save reviewer time, cost per contract, turnaround time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Frontier long-context model needed for whole-contract reasoning; (b) chunk-and-extract with a mid model suffices; (c) split strategy: self-hosted/in-VPC model for restricted customers, API for others; (d) budget is not the real constraint, quality evidence is.
  4. How I'd verify each: Get lawyers to label 60-100 contracts on clause-level ground truth in week 1-2; run 3-4 candidate models with identical task spec; measure clause recall/precision with CIs, cost (18k tokens x 40k = 720M input tokens/year, so even $3/1M in is about $2,160 input cost: cost is negligible vs reviewer time, which is 40k x 25 min = about 16,700 hours), and p95 turnaround.
  5. Root cause: The requirement is underspecified; the economics show quality, not token price, dominates.
  6. Fix: Choose by recall on high-risk clauses first, then cost; design human review for low-confidence items; for restricted customers evaluate a self-hosted or in-tenant option separately and report the quality gap honestly.
  7. Prevention: Keep the labeled set as a regression gate; track missed-clause incidents; plan re-eval on each new model release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not choosing on vendor slides; not optimizing token cost when it is about 0.01 percent of the value at stake; not promising automation without a recall number.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 150k-token contracts exceed the model's effective context? -> Check effective long-context recall (needle-style tests on contract content), else segment with a structure-aware chunker.
  • Budget suddenly capped? -> Cascade: cheap model screens, expensive model verifies flagged clauses.
  • Vendor offers a fine-tuned legal model? -> Test it on your labeled set; domain labeling does not guarantee gains.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team picked a model from a benchmark deck, then lawyers found it missed indemnity carve-outs; after labeling 80 contracts, a cheaper model with a clause-specific prompt beat it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: names a model.
  • Hire: asks clarifying questions, builds a labeled eval, compares candidates.
  • Strong hire: does the economics (cost negligible vs reviewer time), splits by data constraint, defines recall-first criteria.

questions.promptHtml: How do customization options (prompting, RAG, fine-tuning) differ between closed and open-weight models, and how does that affect lock-in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you see that customization assets can be portable or locked to a vendor.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "With open weights I can fully fine-tune, use LoRA, merge, quantize and serve anywhere, and the resulting artifact is mine, subject to the license. Closed vendors offer limited fine-tuning options on selected models, the tuned model lives on their platform and dies with its base model's lifecycle. Prompts and RAG are portable-ish but tuned to a model's quirks. The portable assets are data: eval sets, training examples and retrieval corpora. I invest there."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Asset Portable? Notes
Training/eval datasets Yes Highest value; keep versioned
Prompts Partly Re-tune per model
RAG index (text chunks) Yes Embeddings tied to embed model (see C1 embeddings chunk)
Closed fine-tuned model No Tied to vendor and base lifecycle
Open LoRA adapter Tied to base weights Portable across hosts, not across base models

Rule: fine-tuning is the last lever, after prompting and RAG (see the fine-tuning chunk). If you do tune a closed model, store the dataset so that re-tuning on a new base is a rerun, not a research project.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# portable training record (JSONL), vendor-neutral
{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}], "meta": {"source": "support-2025Q3"}}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Tuning on a closed base with no stored dataset or eval.
  • Believing LoRA adapters transfer across base models.
  • Skipping the baseline: strong prompting plus RAG beats a poor fine-tune.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to a fine-tune when the base is retired? → It is retired too; you must retrain on the successor.
  2. Is open-weight lock-in zero? → No: serving stack, GPU contracts and operational skills lock you in.
  3. How do you reduce prompt lock-in? → Version prompts per model, keep an eval gate, avoid vendor-specific tricks unless needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "open is flexible, closed is locked." Senior: treats datasets and evals as the portable core and lists what each choice ties you to.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's closed fine-tune was retired with its base; the dataset was intact, so the retrain took days, not months.

questions.contextHtml: An AI writing assistant uses a mid-tier closed model (illustrative $2.50 in / $10 out per 1M). Today: 300k requests/day, 900 input and 350 output tokens each. The launch of a new partner will take it to 3M requests/day within a month. API rate limits are 4M tokens/minute today. Quality bar: 85% win-or-tie against the incumbent in blind human pairwise review. Budget owner says the infra bill must not exceed 3x current.
questions.promptHtml: What is your plan to scale 10x?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Ask the vendor for higher limits" and accept 10x cost, or "move everything to a small model."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Request mix by task? Peak-to-average ratio? How much of the prompt is a shared prefix? Latency requirement (interactive vs async)? Which tasks are quality-critical?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Request higher rate limits and a committed-spend discount now (lead time), shorten the shared system prompt, cap output length, enable prompt caching if the provider supports it (verify discount).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) bulk of traffic is simple tasks (grammar, rewrite) a small model handles; (b) caching and prompt trimming cut a large share; (c) tail of hard tasks needs the big model.
  4. How I'd verify each: Cost today: 300k x (900x2.5 + 350x10)/1e6 = 300k x $0.00575 = $1,725/day, so 10x = $17,250/day (about $517k/month) vs a 3x budget of about $5,175/day. Token rate at 10x: 3M x 1,250 tokens = 3.75B tokens/day, averaging 2.6M tokens/min, so peaks at 3x average exceed a 4M/min limit. Classify traffic with a labeled sample; run blind pairwise tests per task category with small vs mid models.
  5. Root cause: Naive linear scaling breaks both the budget and the rate limit.
  6. Fix: Tiered routing by task: small/self-hosted or cheap-tier model for simple tasks, mid model for the rest, rare escalation. If 70% of requests go to a model costing 1/10th: new cost per request = 0.7 x $0.000575 + 0.3 x $0.00575 = $0.0004025 + $0.001725 = $0.002128; x 3M requests = $6,380/day, close to the 3x cap, then caching and output trimming close the gap. Multi-provider capacity for the rate limit.
  7. Prevention: Per-task cost dashboards, quality sampling, rate-limit headroom alerts, load tests before launch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not move everything to small without per-task pairwise evidence; not rely on a single vendor's capacity; not deploy self-hosting in a month without ops readiness.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vendor refuses the limit increase? -> Second provider/region behind the gateway, queue non-urgent work.
  • Win-rate is 80% for the cheap tier on creative tasks? -> Keep those on the mid model; route by task.
  • Cost still 4x? -> Batch/async pricing for background tasks, semantic caching where safe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch hit a rate ceiling at 2.3x load because nobody modeled peak-to-average; requests queued, latency tripled, and a retry storm worsened it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks for more quota; multiplies cost.
  • Hire: computes costs and rate math; proposes routing and caching.
  • Strong hire: validates per-task quality, adds multi-provider capacity, models peaks, and ties to the budget cap.

questions.promptHtml: When should you choose a reasoning model over a standard chat model, and what are the production costs of that choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reasoning models are expensive in tokens and latency; seniors pick them deliberately, not by default.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Reasoning models spend extra inference-time tokens thinking before answering, which helps on multi-step math, code, planning and ambiguous analysis. The cost is hidden thinking tokens, usually billed as output, higher latency, less predictable cost per request, and sometimes weaker instruction-following on simple formats. I use them for hard, high-value tasks, route simple requests to standard models, and cap thinking budget where the API allows."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism (concept level; see the model-architectures and training-stage chunks): reasoning models are trained to produce long chains of thought, so quality scales with test-time compute. Billing: thinking tokens typically count as output tokens even if hidden from you (verify the provider's billing page). Example (illustrative price $10/1M output): a standard answer of 300 tokens costs $0.003; a reasoning answer with 4,000 thinking + 300 visible tokens costs $0.043, about 14x. Latency: at 40 ms/token, 4,300 tokens is about 172 s of decoding versus 12 s, so you need streaming progress, async jobs or lower effort settings.

Selection rubric: use reasoning when (1) correctness depends on multi-step derivation, (2) verification is expensive downstream, (3) latency tolerance is seconds-to-minutes, (4) volume is low or value per request high. Avoid for classification, extraction, rewriting, chit-chat, and strict-format high-QPS tasks, where a small model plus validation wins.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def choose(task):
    if task.needs_multistep and task.latency_budget_s > 30 and task.value_usd > 0.5:
        return "reasoning"
    return "standard"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting thinking tokens when estimating cost and max_tokens (a cap can cut off the answer after thinking).
  • Using reasoning models for simple extraction and paying 10x for the same accuracy.
  • Assuming chain-of-thought text shown is a faithful explanation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you control cost? → Effort/budget settings where offered, routing by difficulty, output caps, caching.
  2. Can a standard model plus a verifier match it? → Often for verifiable tasks; compare cost per correct answer.
  3. How do you evaluate? → Cost per correct answer and p95 latency on a hard slice, not average score.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "reasoning models are smarter, use them." Senior: computes cost per correct answer, handles latency UX, and routes by difficulty.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team switched a ticket classifier to a reasoning model; accuracy was unchanged, cost rose 9x, and p95 went from 2 s to 25 s.
